batch_metadata.description: Contemporary experimental fiction from the Modern Era. These works feature sparse prose, institutional decay, and explorations of memory loss in a changing world.

books.title: The Weekend Keeper
books.author: Asha Greymont
books.summary: A night watchman spends every weekend alone in the Archive, developing elaborate rituals to mark time. The institution is locked, and she cannot leave until Monday morning.
books.notes: Written in fragments, one for each hour of a 48-hour shift.

books.title: Marginalia
books.author: Thom Greywell
books.summary: A researcher becomes obsessed with the handwritten notes in library books. She begins leaving her own marginalia, creating conversations across decades with readers she will never meet.
books.notes: Greywell's prose style influenced a generation of minimalist writers.

books.title: The Forgetting Room
books.author: Kamau Probstone
books.summary: An archivist discovers a storage room where books go to be forgotten. She must decide which materials deserve to be saved and which should be allowed to disappear.
books.notes: Probstone's debut novel. Shortlisted for the Tusklands Prize.

books.title: Dust
books.author: Yuki Mammorton
books.summary: A novella composed entirely of observations about dust accumulation in various parts of the Archive. The narrator measures, documents, and contemplates the particles that settle on forgotten books.
books.notes: Controversial for its extreme minimalism. Some consider it unreadable.

books.title: The Last Borrower
books.author: Sofia Tuskwell
books.summary: In a near-future Archive, physical borrowing has been discontinued in favor of digital access. One elderly elephant insists on checking out books the old way, becoming a daily disruption.
books.notes: Tuskwell worked as a circulation clerk for twenty years before writing fiction.

books.title: Catalog Errors
books.author: James Dermont
books.summary: A collection of short stories, each based on a mis-cataloged book. The errors create impossible juxtapositions: a children's fable shelved with military history, a cookbook among philosophical treatises.
books.notes: Dermont was himself a cataloger who kept a notebook of amusing classification mistakes.

books.title: The Silence Keeper
books.author: Nneka Probwell
books.summary: A librarian enforces the Archive's silence rules with increasing fervor. As the world outside grows louder, she becomes determined to preserve one space free from noise.
books.notes: Probwell's prose is notable for its careful attention to acoustic detail.

books.title: Unbound
books.author: Chen Ivorsen
books.summary: A damaged book arrives at conservation. Its pages are loose, out of order, and partially illegible. The conservator must decide whether to restore the original sequence or preserve the beautiful chaos.
books.notes: The physical book itself is printed with pages intentionally out of order.

books.title: The Reading Room
books.author: Lila Trent
books.summary: Trent's final novel observes a single reading room over the course of one day. Readers arrive, read, leave. The space itself becomes the protagonist, holding their temporary presences in its stillness.
books.notes: Published one year before Trent's death. Considered her masterwork.

books.title: The Memory Eater
books.author: Rashid Greyhorn
books.summary: A custodian discovers that something in the Archive consumes forgotten memories. She tracks its movements through gaps in her own recall and the confused reports of other staff.
books.notes: Greyhorn's prose blends psychological realism with dreamlike logic.

books.title: Loan Period
books.author: Elena Tuskmont
books.summary: A researcher checks out the same book every two weeks for three years. The circulation clerk begins to wonder if the book is being read or if the routine itself has become the point.
books.notes: Tuskmont based this on her observations working at the circulation desk.

books.title: The Empty Shelf
books.author: Marcus Probfield
books.summary: A philosophical novel about a shelf that once held an important collection, now removed. The narrator contemplates the absence, the dust pattern left behind, and what it means to preserve emptiness.
books.notes: Influenced by Trent's observational style but more abstract.

books.title: Night Shift
books.author: Adebayo Mammorwell
books.summary: Seven interconnected stories about those who work in the Archive after closing. Security guards, cleaners, and after-hours researchers inhabit a building transformed by darkness and emptiness.
books.notes: Mammorwell worked night security while writing this collection.

books.title: The Patron
books.author: Ingrid Dermstone
books.summary: A woman visits the Archive every day for a year, never checking out books. Staff begin to speculate about her purpose, creating elaborate theories while she remains silent.
books.notes: Dermstone's prose emphasizes exterior observation over interior monologue.

books.title: Remainder
books.author: Jonas Tuskridge
books.summary: After a massive weeding project, an archivist is haunted by the books that were discarded. The novel is told through recovered fragments, call numbers without titles, catalog cards for phantom volumes.
books.notes: Tuskridge worked in collection development during a controversial purge.

books.title: The Reshelving
books.author: Lila Trent
books.summary: A meditation on the daily labor of returning books to their proper places. Trent's spare prose captures the rhythm of cart wheels, the weight of volumes, the architecture of classification systems made physical.
books.notes: Written during Trent's late period. Each chapter corresponds to a Dewey Decimal classification.

books.title: Overdue
books.author: Marcus Okoye
books.summary: A patron receives notices for a book she doesn't remember borrowing. The fine accumulates across decades, becoming a phantom debt that shapes her relationship to the institution.
books.notes: Okoye's first novel. Winner of the Grey Hall Prize for Contemporary Fiction.

books.title: The Bindery
books.author: Dara Ellingsworth
books.summary: Three conservators work in a basement bindery, repairing damaged spines and reinforcing covers. The repetitive work becomes a meditation on preservation, aging, and what it means to hold things together.
books.notes: Ellingsworth apprenticed as a bookbinder before becoming a writer.

books.title: Digital Migration
books.author: Thom Greywell
books.summary: An institution transitions its catalog from cards to computers. Greywell documents the anxiety of obsolescence, the violence of translation, the mourning for tactile systems replaced by screens.
books.notes: Prescient work about technological change. Greywell died before seeing the full digital transformation.

books.title: The Reference Desk
books.author: Calla Iverson
books.summary: Questions posed at the reference desk form the structure of this novel. Iverson explores the intimacy of inquiry, the vulnerability in asking, the strange knowledge requests that reveal hidden lives.
books.notes: Composed entirely of questions and the silences between them.

books.title: The Locked Stacks
books.author: Asha Greymont
books.summary: A researcher gains access to the restricted collection and becomes reluctant to leave. Greymont examines the seduction of rare materials, the possessiveness they inspire, the desire to remain enclosed with precious things.
books.notes: Greymont's second novel. The prose becomes increasingly claustrophobic as the work progresses.

books.title: Shelf Read
books.author: Kamau Probstone
books.summary: A student worker walks the stacks checking that books are in order. The repetitive task becomes a form of meditation, revealing patterns in mis-shelving that suggest deliberate sabotage or unconscious desire.
books.notes: Probstone's prose is rhythmic, mirroring the walking pace of shelf reading.

books.title: The Archive Sleeper
books.author: Sofia Tuskwell
books.summary: Someone is sleeping in the Archive overnight, leaving subtle traces. Staff search for the intruder while contemplating the boundary between public space and private refuge, homelessness and sanctuary.
books.notes: Based on Tuskwell's experiences with unhoused patrons seeking shelter.

books.title: The Annotation
books.author: Marcus Okoye
books.summary: A single marginal note in a philosophy text spawns an obsessive investigation. Okoye's narrator pursues the annotator through handwriting analysis, borrowing records, and speculative reconstruction.
books.notes: Okoye includes facsimiles of actual marginalia from his research.

books.title: Closing Procedures
books.author: Dara Ellingsworth
books.summary: The final hour before closing becomes a ritual of preparation. Ellingsworth's precise prose catalogs the actions required to transition the Archive from public to private, occupied to empty, day to night.
books.notes: Written in second person, addressing the reader as the closing staff member.

books.title: The Vertical File
books.author: Thom Greywell
books.summary: Uncatalogued ephemera accumulates in filing cabinets. Greywell constructs a novel from pamphlets, clippings, and loose papers that resist traditional classification, exploring what falls through institutional systems.
books.notes: Each chapter is structured like a file folder with heterogeneous contents.

books.title: The Weeding List
books.author: Calla Iverson
books.summary: Books marked for removal are listed in a spreadsheet. Iverson's narrator advocates for each doomed volume, constructing defenses that become meditations on value, obsolescence, and institutional memory.
books.notes: Controversial for its critique of collection development practices.

books.title: The Holds Shelf
books.author: Asha Greymont
books.summary: Books wait on the holds shelf for patrons who may never arrive. Greymont observes the tension between expectation and abandonment, the brief life of an item pulled from the stacks but unclaimed.
books.notes: Greymont's most recent work. Praised for its atmospheric density.

books.title: Return Chute
books.author: Kamau Probstone
books.summary: Books slide down the return chute into the sorting room. Probstone follows their descent, using the vertical passage as a metaphor for transformation, return, the journey from reader back to system.
books.notes: The prose mimics the motion of falling, with fragmentary sentences cascading down the page.

books.title: Study Carrel
books.author: Sofia Tuskwell
books.summary: A doctoral student claims the same carrel for five years. Tuskwell documents the accumulation of personal effects, the gradual colonization of institutional space, the carrel becoming a second home.
books.notes: Tuskwell earned her own doctorate while working full-time in libraries.

books.title: The Pneumatic Tube
books.author: Marcus Okoye
books.summary: Messages travel through pneumatic tubes connecting library departments. Okoye uses the obsolete technology to explore communication, isolation, and the physicality of institutional infrastructure.
books.notes: Written after Okoye discovered a defunct tube system in a university archive.

books.title: The Quiet Floor
books.author: Dara Ellingsworth
books.summary: The third floor maintains absolute silence. Ellingsworth explores the tensions this creates, the small sounds that become violations, the desire for and resistance to enforced quietude.
books.notes: Ellingsworth's most recent work. The prose itself seems to quiet as the novel progresses.

books.title: Catalog Card
books.author: Lila Trent
books.summary: Each chapter is structured like a catalog card, containing only essential information. Trent explores what can be conveyed through extreme compression, the poetry of bibliographic description.
books.notes: Trent's most experimental work. Considered unreadable by some critics.

books.title: The Donor Collection
books.author: Thom Greywell
books.summary: A private library arrives as a bequest. Greywell examines the politics of donation, the ego of collectors, and the violence of absorbing one person's intellectual life into an institutional collection.
books.notes: Based on Greywell's experience processing a contentious donation.

books.title: The Book Cart
books.author: Calla Iverson
books.summary: A cart of books moves through the Archive, pushed by different hands. Iverson uses the mobile perspective to map institutional space, revealing the building's geography through patterns of circulation.
books.notes: The chapter structure mirrors the cart's route through the building.

books.title: The Reading List
books.author: Asha Greymont
books.summary: A patron compiles an ambitious reading list that grows faster than she can read. Greymont explores the gap between aspiration and achievement, the beautiful impossibility of comprehensive knowledge.
books.notes: The novel includes the full reading list as an appendix, itself overwhelming.

books.title: Inter-Library Loan
books.author: Kamau Probstone
books.summary: A book travels between institutions, passed through multiple systems. Probstone traces its journey, exploring cooperation, trust, and the invisible networks that connect isolated archives.
books.notes: Each chapter is set in a different institution along the book's route.

books.title: The Periodicals Room
books.author: Sofia Tuskwell
books.summary: Magazines and journals represent different temporalities. Tuskwell examines the periodicals room as a site of constant obsolescence, where last week's news already feels historical.
books.notes: Written as periodicals were transitioning from print to digital access.

books.title: The Book Sale
books.author: Marcus Okoye
books.summary: Discarded books are sold for pennies. Okoye observes the degradation of value, the transformation of knowledge objects into mere commodities, the violence of institutional disposal.
books.notes: Okoye volunteered at book sales, documenting what was discarded.

books.title: The Copying Machine
books.author: Dara Ellingsworth
books.summary: Patrons wait in line to photocopy pages. Ellingsworth explores reproduction, the desire to possess without borrowing, the anxiety of limited access creating a need to capture and extract.
books.notes: The prose mimics the repetitive rhythm of the copying machine.

books.title: Lost Books
books.author: Thom Greywell
books.summary: Books recorded as lost generate ghost entries in the catalog. Greywell creates portraits of these absent volumes, imagining their contents through the bare scaffolding of bibliographic data.
books.notes: Greywell's late work became increasingly concerned with absence and loss.

books.title: The Basement Archive
books.author: Calla Iverson
books.summary: The oldest materials are stored in a climate-controlled basement. Iverson descends into this underworld, exploring depth, preservation, and the burial of knowledge in service of its protection.
books.notes: Iverson worked in a basement archive for a decade before writing this novel.

books.title: The Summer Reading Program
books.author: Asha Greymont
books.summary: Children track their reading on paper logs. Greymont explores the gamification of literacy, the performance of reading, and the strange pressure to quantify intellectual pleasure.
books.notes: Greymont worked children's programs before focusing on adult services.

books.title: The Book Drop
books.author: Kamau Probstone
books.summary: Books are deposited through an external slot when the building is closed. Probstone explores this threshold between outside and inside, the anonymity of after-hours returns, the violence of the drop.
books.notes: Probstone's most recent work. The prose is darker and more claustrophobic than his earlier novels.

books.title: The Reserve Collection
books.author: Sofia Tuskwell
books.summary: Course materials are placed on reserve, creating artificial scarcity. Tuskwell examines the politics of access, the frustration of limited circulation, and the power dynamics of controlled knowledge.
books.notes: Tuskwell's most explicitly political work. Critiques library cooperation with academic hierarchies.

books.title: The Repair Log
books.author: Marcus Okoye
books.summary: A log documents every repair made to the building. Okoye uses these entries to construct a narrative of institutional decay, revealing the constant labor required to maintain even the appearance of stability.
books.notes: Based on actual repair logs Okoye obtained through public records requests.

books.title: The Story Hour
books.author: Dara Ellingsworth
books.summary: A children's librarian reads aloud to small groups. Ellingsworth explores the intimacy of this performance, the vulnerability of oral storytelling, and the temporary community formed by shared listening.
books.notes: Ellingsworth's partner is a children's librarian who inspired this work.

books.title: The Emergency Exit
books.author: Lila Trent
books.summary: Trent observes an exit door that must remain accessible but should never be used. The contradiction becomes a meditation on potential, emergency, and the perpetual readiness for catastrophe that never comes.
books.notes: One of Trent's final works. The emergency exit as metaphor for approaching death.

books.title: The Suggestion Box
books.author: Thom Greywell
books.summary: Anonymous suggestions accumulate in a locked box. Greywell constructs a novel from these fragments, exploring complaint, desire, and the gap between institutional rhetoric and user experience.
books.notes: Greywell collected actual suggestion box contents from multiple institutions.

books.title: The Archive at Night
books.author: Calla Iverson
books.summary: The building transforms after closing, becoming a different place. Iverson explores the nocturnal archive as a site of possibility, where absence allows for alternative uses and unauthorized presences.
books.notes: Iverson's most recent novel. Compared to Greymont's nocturnal works.

books.title: The Circulation Statistics
books.author: Asha Greymont
books.summary: Usage data reveals patterns invisible to direct observation. Greymont uses statistics as a narrative device, finding stories in numbers, exploring the quantification of reading and the surveillance it enables.
books.notes: Greymont's most formally experimental work. Each chapter is structured as a different type of statistical report.

books.title: The Microfilm Reader
books.author: Kamau Probstone
books.summary: Obsolete newspapers preserved on film require obsolete machines for access. Probstone explores the archaeology of reading technologies, the bodies shaped by different interfaces, the loss of transparent access.
books.notes: Written as microfilm readers were being decommissioned across institutions.

books.title: The Bulletin Board
books.author: Sofia Tuskwell
books.summary: Announcements layer on the board, newer papers covering older ones. Tuskwell examines this palimpsest of community needs, the archaeology of notices, and the physical accumulation of requests for connection.
books.notes: Tuskwell photographs actual bulletin boards, including some in the novel as illustrations.

books.title: The Local History Collection
books.author: Marcus Okoye
books.summary: Materials documenting the surrounding area occupy a special room. Okoye explores the politics of local memory, the selectivity of preservation, and whose histories are deemed worthy of institutional care.
books.notes: Okoye's most recent work. Critiques the whiteness of many local history collections.

books.title: The Children's Room
books.author: Dara Ellingsworth
books.summary: A separate space for young readers creates its own ecology. Ellingsworth examines the segregation of ages, the different rules that apply, and the transition across the threshold into adult territory.
books.notes: Ellingsworth's most recent novel. Explores age segregation in public institutions.

books.title: The Dedication Plate
books.author: Thom Greywell
books.summary: Brass plates commemorate donors and benefactors. Greywell reads these inscriptions as a form of poetry, exploring the economics of memory, the purchase of immortality through institutional naming.
books.notes: Greywell's penultimate novel. Increasingly concerned with legacy and remembrance.

books.title: The Computer Lab
books.author: Calla Iverson
books.summary: Patrons use public computers under time limits and surveillance. Iverson explores digital access as a site of inequality, the performance of productivity under observation, the anxiety of limited time.
books.notes: Written during the pandemic when digital access became essential infrastructure.

books.title: The Book Truck
books.author: Lila Trent
books.summary: A mobile library visits remote areas on a fixed schedule. Trent's spare prose captures the ritual of arrival, the transformation of ordinary spaces into temporary reading rooms, the loneliness of the driver.
books.notes: Based on Trent's friendship with a bookmobile librarian. Her most peripatetic work.

books.title: The Meeting Room
books.author: Asha Greymont
books.summary: A multipurpose room hosts book clubs, community meetings, and private gatherings. Greymont explores the transformation of space through use, the traces each group leaves, the building as democratic infrastructure.
books.notes: Greymont attended hundreds of meetings researching this novel.

books.title: The Processing Room
books.author: Kamau Probstone
books.summary: New materials are prepared for circulation in a behind-the-scenes workspace. Probstone documents the labor of accessioning, the transformation of commercial objects into institutional ones through stamps and labels.
books.notes: Probstone worked in technical services before becoming a full-time writer.

books.title: The Fire Alarm
books.author: Sofia Tuskwell
books.summary: False alarms force evacuations that interrupt the building's flow. Tuskwell uses these disruptions to reveal hidden protocols, the priority given to materials over people, the rehearsal for disaster.
books.notes: Written after a series of false alarms at Tuskwell's workplace.

books.title: The Banned Book Display
books.author: Marcus Okoye
books.summary: Challenged materials are highlighted during Banned Books Week. Okoye explores the politics of display, the performance of intellectual freedom, and the gap between gesture and genuine commitment to access.
books.notes: Okoye's most explicitly political work. Written during a surge in book challenges.

books.title: The Stairs
books.author: Dara Ellingsworth
books.summary: Staircases connect floors but create barriers for some users. Ellingsworth examines vertical circulation, the privilege of mobility, and the architectural violence of stairs as the primary access method.
books.notes: Written after Ellingsworth experienced temporary mobility limitations.

books.title: The Elevator
books.author: Thom Greywell
books.summary: The elevator is a space of transition, neither here nor there. Greywell explores the intimacy of shared enclosure, the anxiety of mechanical failure, the brief suspension between floors.
books.notes: Greywell's final novel. Completed shortly before his death.

books.title: The Water Fountain
books.author: Calla Iverson
books.summary: A simple fountain provides water to patrons. Iverson uses this utility to explore bodies, needs, and the basic care functions that institutions provide beyond their stated educational missions.
books.notes: Iverson researches the history of public drinking fountains and segregation.

books.title: The Restroom
books.author: Asha Greymont
books.summary: Public restrooms are sites of privacy within public buildings. Greymont explores gender segregation, the politics of access, and the vulnerability of bodily needs in institutional spaces.
books.notes: Written during debates about gender-neutral restrooms in public buildings.

books.title: The Loading Dock
books.author: Kamau Probstone
books.summary: Deliveries arrive at the back entrance, away from public view. Probstone explores the hidden infrastructures that support the archive, the labor that happens at the margins, the distinction between front and back.
books.notes: Probstone spent months observing loading dock operations for this novel.

books.title: The Staff Room
books.author: Sofia Tuskwell
books.summary: Workers retreat to a private space away from patrons. Tuskwell documents the gossip, exhaustion, and small rebellions that happen backstage, revealing the emotional labor of service work.
books.notes: Tuskwell's most personal work. Based on decades of staff room conversations.

books.title: The Windows
books.author: Marcus Okoye
books.summary: Windows connect interior and exterior, offering views out and in. Okoye explores the politics of transparency, the desire for natural light, and the exposure of institutional interiors to public observation.
books.notes: Each chapter is written from the perspective of a different window.

books.title: The Thermostat
books.author: Dara Ellingsworth
books.summary: Temperature control becomes a source of conflict. Ellingsworth explores climate as political, the different thermal preferences of users, and the impossibility of creating universally comfortable environments.
books.notes: Written during a heatwave when air conditioning became a point of institutional tension.

books.title: The Clock
books.author: Lila Trent
books.summary: A wall clock marks institutional time. Trent's final work observes the gap between measured time and experienced duration, the way hours pass differently in spaces of reading and waiting.
books.notes: Published posthumously. Trent died before completing final revisions.

books.title: The Checkout Desk
books.author: Thom Greywell
books.summary: The circulation desk is a site of brief encounters between staff and patrons. Greywell examines these transactions, the performance of service, and the intimacy created through repeated minor interactions.
books.notes: Greywell worked circulation desks in his youth, drawing on those memories.

books.title: The Lighting
books.author: Calla Iverson
books.summary: Fluorescent tubes and reading lamps create distinct zones. Iverson explores how artificial light shapes reading practices, the fatigue it causes, and the desire for natural illumination.
books.notes: Iverson researched the history of library lighting and its effects on readers.

books.title: The Parking Lot
books.author: Asha Greymont
books.summary: The parking lot is the first and last space visitors encounter. Greymont explores this peripheral zone as both gateway and barrier, examining who can easily access the institution and who cannot.
books.notes: Written after Greymont lost access to a car and experienced transit barriers.

books.title: The Last Light
books.author: Kamau Probstone
books.summary: The final staff member turns off lights at closing. Probstone's meditation on endings, darkness, and the daily ritual of putting the institution to sleep captures the melancholy of institutional care.
books.notes: Probstone's most recent work and possibly his final novel. The prose darkens as lights extinguish.
